modules.title: Time matters: prepayments & deferrals
modules.summary: Use a timeline to match expenses to the period they belong to.

sections.title: Cash timing is not expense timing
sections.text: Accrual accounting recognises expenses in the period they relate to, not simply when cash is paid. A deferral moves an amount recorded or received now into a later period. A prepayment is the asset representing a benefit paid for but not yet used.
sections.new: Paying for a year of insurance is like buying twelve monthly slices. Only the slices used this year are this year's expense.

sections.title: Draw the dates first
sections.text: Identify the reporting year-end and the coverage period. Count the months used and the months still to come. Allocate evenly only if the question says or implies the benefit is spread evenly. A cash payment for future coverage is not automatically all this year's expense.
sections.new: Draw a line from the start to the end of the policy and put a mark at year-end. The part after the mark is still an asset.

sections.title: Adjust an expense already recorded
sections.text: If the full payment was debited to expense, the year-end adjustment is Dr Prepayments, Cr Expense for the unused part. Current expense = cash paid + opening prepayment − closing prepayment, assuming no accruals and that the opening prepayment is used this year.
sections.new: The credit removes the unused cost from expense. The debit parks it as a benefit for next year.

example.prompt: On 1 October, pay £1,200 for 12 months' insurance and debit Insurance expense. Year-end is 31 December. Cover is even.
steps: Adjust: Dr Prepayments £900; Cr Insurance expense £900.
example.result: SoFP current asset £900; income statement insurance expense £300.

modules.watch: Do not debit Bank at the year-end adjustment: the cash payment happened earlier.

terms.definition: Postponing recognition to a later period when cash or an initial recording comes first.
An asset for an expense paid before its benefit is used.

questions.q: A prepayment for unused insurance is normally:
questions.explain: The business has paid for a benefit it will receive in a future period, creating an asset.
questions.hint: Has the business already paid for a future benefit?

questions.q: £600 of rent recorded as expense relates to next year. Which adjustment?
questions.explain: Debit prepayments to recognise the future benefit; credit rent to reduce this year's expense.
questions.hint: Move the future portion out of expense and into an asset.

questions.q: Pay £2,400 for 12 months from 1 July. Year-end 31 December; even cover. Current-year expense?
questions.explain: Six months are used: £2,400 × 6/12 = £1,200.
questions.hint: Count July to December inclusive.

questions.q: What is a deferral?
options: Moving recognition to a later period after advance payment or receipt
questions.explain: Deferrals include prepaid expenses and income received before it is earned.
questions.hint: Cash comes before the related expense or income is recognised.

questions.q: An adjustment credits Insurance expense £300. What is the effect on profit, all else equal?
questions.explain: The credit reduces an expense, so profit increases by £300 compared with the unadjusted figure.
questions.hint: Lower expenses mean higher profit.

questions.q: Why is Bank not credited again for a prepayment adjustment?
options: No new payment occurs at the adjustment date
questions.explain: The cash movement was recorded when paid. The adjustment reallocates an expense to an asset.
questions.hint: Separate the original payment from the year-end timing correction.

questions.q: Cash insurance £1,500; opening prepayment £200 fully used; closing prepayment £350. Expense, with no accruals?
questions.explain: £1,500 + £200 − £350 = £1,350. Include this year's use of last year's prepayment.
questions.hint: Add opening prepayment used, subtract closing prepayment unused.

questions.q: Pay £900 on 1 November for 6 months' cover, charged to expense. Year-end 31 December. Adjustment amount?
questions.explain: Two months used, four months remain: £900 × 4/6 = £600 prepaid.
questions.hint: The adjustment is for unused months, not the months already consumed.

modules.title: Accruals & income received in advance
modules.summary: Recognise costs owed, income earned and income that is not yet earned.

sections.title: Expenses incurred but not yet paid
sections.text: An expense accrual recognises a cost already incurred that is missing from the accounts: Dr Expense, Cr Accruals. The accrual is normally a current liability. Expense = cash paid + closing accrual − opening accrual where there are no prepayments and opening accruals are settled in cash paid.
sections.new: You used electricity in December but the bill comes in January. December still gets the expense and a record that payment is owed.

sections.title: Income earned but not received
sections.text: Accrued income is an asset for income earned but not yet received or recorded: Dr Accrued income, Cr Income. It is the mirror of an expense accrual. Do not assume every use of the word 'accrual' means a liability.
sections.new: You have done the work and earned the money, but it has not reached the bank. Record both the income and the right to collect it.

sections.title: Income received before it is earned
sections.text: Prepaid income, deferred income or income received in advance is a liability when performance is still owed. If the receipt was initially credited to Sales, adjust Dr Sales, Cr Income received in advance. If recorded correctly as a liability on receipt, do not defer it twice. Release it to income when earned.
sections.new: A customer pays now for next month's service. The business owes a service, so the money is not yet this month's income.

example.prompt: At year-end, unrecorded electricity used is £240. A £600 customer receipt credited to Sales includes £200 for next year's services.
steps: Expense accrual: Dr Electricity expense £240; Cr Accruals £240.
Income deferral: Dr Sales £200; Cr Income received in advance £200.
Profit falls £440 compared with the unadjusted accounts; liabilities rise £440.
example.result: A liability can mean an obligation to pay cash or an obligation to provide a service.

modules.watch: Prepaid expense is an asset; prepaid income is a liability. Always ask which side of the service the business is on.

terms.definition: A liability for an expense incurred but not yet paid or recorded.
An asset for income already earned but not yet received or recorded.

reading.topics: Income recognition; accrued expenses; accrued and deferred income

questions.q: £180 electricity has been used but not recorded or paid. Adjustment?
questions.explain: Recognise the cost and an obligation to pay. Bank is unchanged at the adjustment date.
questions.hint: The cost belongs here, even though cash leaves later.

questions.q: An expense accrual is normally:
questions.explain: The business owes payment for a benefit already consumed.
questions.hint: Think 'we owe for a cost already used'.

questions.q: £500 earned service income is not yet recorded or received. Which entry?
options: Dr Accrued income; Cr Service income
questions.explain: Accrued income is an asset; credit income to recognise the amount earned.
questions.hint: The business has a right to collect for work already done.

questions.q: £300 credited to Sales relates entirely to services next year. Adjustment?
options: Dr Income in advance; Cr Sales
Dr Sales; Cr Income in advance
questions.explain: Remove the unearned revenue with a debit and recognise a liability with a credit.
questions.hint: The service is still owed to the customer.

questions.q: Income received in advance is a liability because:
options: The business still owes the promised service or goods
questions.explain: The obligation is to perform for the customer, not necessarily to refund cash.
questions.hint: What has the business promised but not yet delivered?

questions.q: Recording a previously missing £400 expense accrual does what to profit?
questions.explain: The new expense reduces profit £400 while the accrual increases liabilities £400.
questions.hint: An extra expense has been recognised.

questions.q: Cash wages paid £8,000, opening accrual £500 settled in that cash, closing accrual £700. Wages expense?
questions.explain: £8,000 − £500 + £700 = £8,200. Exclude last year's cost and include this year's unpaid cost.
questions.hint: Cash paid + closing accrual − opening accrual.

questions.q: Current-year service cash receipts £2,000; opening deferred income £300 is now earned; closing deferred income £500. No receivables. Current revenue?
questions.explain: Revenue = current cash £2,000 + opening deferred income earned £300 − closing unearned income £500 = £1,800. The opening amount is prior cash, released this year.
questions.hint: Add last year's cash now earned, remove this year's cash not yet earned.

modules.title: Depreciation & carrying amounts
modules.summary: Allocate asset cost over useful life and keep cash separate from expense.

sections.title: Allocate cost, not market value
sections.text: Depreciation systematically allocates the depreciable amount of property, plant and equipment over its useful life. It is not a cash reserve or a calculation of resale price. Depreciable amount = cost − estimated residual value. Land is normally not depreciated; limited-life buildings and equipment are.
sections.new: An asset helps earn income over several years. Rather than charging all its cost in one year, share its depreciable cost across the periods that use it.

sections.title: Straight-line and the annual entry
sections.text: Straight-line annual depreciation = (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life. Apply time apportionment if the stated policy requires it. Record Dr Depreciation expense, Cr Accumulated depreciation. The asset's cost stays in its cost account. Carrying amount, or net book value (NBV), = cost − accumulated depreciation in these examples.
sections.new: Keep two records: what it originally cost, and how much has been charged so far. The difference is the amount still carried as an asset.

sections.title: Related allocation terms
sections.text: Finite-life intangible assets are amortised. Natural resources may use depletion. Indefinite-life intangible assets are not automatically amortised; their treatment depends on the applicable framework. For reducing-balance depreciation, apply the stated percentage to opening carrying amount, not original cost each year.
sections.new: The label depends on the kind of asset. For this course, focus first on the idea of sharing an asset's cost across the periods using it.

example.prompt: Equipment costs £6,000, has residual value £600 and a 3-year useful life. Assume a full year's straight-line charge.
steps: Entry: Dr Depreciation expense £1,800; Cr Accumulated depreciation £1,800.
After two full years: accumulated depreciation £3,600; carrying amount £2,400.
example.result: Depreciation reduces profit and carrying amount, but does not itself move cash.

modules.watch: Do not credit Bank for depreciation. Bank was affected when the asset was purchased.

terms.definition: The estimated disposal proceeds at the end of useful life, less estimated disposal costs.
Total depreciation charged on an asset to date; a contra-asset account.

reading.topics: Capital expenditure; depreciation methods; non-current assets

questions.q: Cost £5,000, residual value £500, useful life 5 years. Annual straight-line depreciation?
questions.hint: Deduct residual value before dividing by useful life.

questions.q: Which is the normal depreciation entry?
options: Dr Depreciation expense; Cr Accumulated depreciation
questions.explain: The debit records an expense; the credit builds a contra-asset balance.
questions.hint: Cost allocation is an expense, not a cash payment.

questions.q: Equipment cost £8,000 and accumulated depreciation £3,200. Carrying amount?
questions.hint: Accumulated depreciation reduces the original cost.

questions.q: Depreciation is primarily:
options: An exact measure of market value
Allocation of depreciable cost over useful life
questions.explain: Depreciation matches asset cost to periods of use; it does not set aside cash or directly measure value.
questions.hint: Think cost allocation, not valuation.

questions.q: Which term usually describes cost allocation for a finite-life intangible asset?
questions.explain: Amortisation applies to finite-life intangibles; depreciation to PPE, and depletion to natural resources.
questions.hint: The asset has no physical substance.

questions.q: Which account normally remains unchanged by the annual depreciation journal?
questions.explain: The allocation is non-cash. It changes expense and accumulated depreciation, with a profit effect.
questions.hint: No new cash payment happens when recording the annual charge.

questions.q: Equipment £12,000, no residual value, 4-year life. Bought 1 October; 31 December year-end. Monthly apportionment. Charge?
questions.explain: Annual charge £3,000, then 3/12 of a year = £750.
questions.hint: First calculate a full year's expense, then take three months.

questions.q: Opening carrying amount £4,000, reducing-balance rate 25%. This year's depreciation?
questions.explain: £4,000 × 25% = £1,000. Reducing balance uses the opening carrying amount.
questions.hint: Apply the percentage to the remaining carrying amount.

modules.title: Disposing of non-current assets
modules.summary: Remove cost and accumulated depreciation, then find the gain or loss.

sections.title: Find carrying amount at the sale date
sections.text: Before disposal, record any depreciation required by the question up to disposal. Carrying amount = original cost − accumulated depreciation at that date. Compare net proceeds with carrying amount, not original cost. Proceeds above carrying amount create a gain; proceeds below it create a loss.
sections.new: The asset no longer sits in the accounts at its original cost net of nothing. Compare what you get with what is still left in the accounts.

sections.title: Use a disposal clearing account
sections.text: Transfer original cost: Dr Disposal, Cr Asset cost. Transfer that asset's accumulated depreciation: Dr Accumulated depreciation, Cr Disposal. Record proceeds: Dr Bank, Cr Disposal. Use only the depreciation relating to the asset sold, not all assets in that class.
sections.new: The disposal account gathers three pieces: original cost on the debit side, and depreciation already charged plus sale proceeds on the credit side.

sections.title: Clear the gain or loss
sections.text: A remaining debit balance in Disposal is a loss: Dr Loss on disposal, Cr Disposal. A remaining credit balance is a gain: Dr Disposal, Cr Gain on disposal. The gain or loss affects the income statement. After closing, Disposal is nil and the sold asset is removed from the SoFP.
sections.new: The disposal account is a temporary working area. Move its final difference to profit or loss so the working area is empty again.

example.prompt: Sell a van for £3,000. Original cost £10,000; accumulated depreciation at sale £6,000.
steps: Dr Disposal £10,000; Cr Motor vehicles cost £10,000.
Disposal has £1,000 net debit: Dr Loss on disposal £1,000; Cr Disposal £1,000.

modules.watch: The credit to the asset cost account removes its original cost, not just its carrying amount.

terms.definition: A temporary account collecting cost, accumulated depreciation and proceeds to calculate a disposal result.
Net proceeds exceeding the carrying amount of the asset sold.

reading.topics: Non-current asset disposals; gain or loss on sale

questions.q: Cost £9,000; accumulated depreciation £6,000; proceeds £2,500. Disposal result?
questions.explain: Carrying amount is £3,000. Receiving £2,500 creates a £500 loss.
questions.hint: Compare proceeds with cost less accumulated depreciation.

questions.q: To remove an asset's original cost on disposal, use:
questions.explain: Debit Disposal and credit the asset cost account for its original cost.
questions.hint: The cost account normally has a debit balance, so removing cost needs a credit.

questions.q: To transfer the sold asset's accumulated depreciation, use:
questions.explain: Debit accumulated depreciation to remove its credit balance; credit Disposal.
questions.hint: Remove the contra-asset balance relating to the asset sold.

questions.q: Cash proceeds from sale of a non-current asset are recorded as:
questions.explain: Bank increases, and the proceeds are credited to the disposal clearing account.
questions.hint: The sale receipt is one of the credits in the disposal account.

questions.q: After cost, depreciation and proceeds are posted, Disposal has a £700 debit balance. This is:
questions.explain: A remaining debit means proceeds were below carrying amount: a loss of £700.
questions.hint: Debits exceeding credits leave unrecovered carrying cost.

questions.q: Cost £4,000, accumulated depreciation £2,500, proceeds £1,800. Gain or loss?
questions.explain: Carrying amount is £1,500. Proceeds £1,800 exceed it by £300.
questions.hint: Profit on sale is not calculated against original cost alone.

questions.q: Opening carrying amount £5,000. Depreciation to disposal £500; net proceeds £4,600. Result?
questions.explain: Carrying amount at sale is £4,500; £4,600 proceeds give a £100 gain.
questions.hint: Update carrying amount to the disposal date first.

questions.q: How do you close a £200 credit balance on Disposal?
options: Dr Gain on disposal; Cr Disposal
Dr Disposal; Cr Gain on disposal
Dr Loss on disposal; Cr Bank
questions.explain: Debit Disposal to clear its credit balance, and credit gain on disposal in profit or loss.
questions.hint: A credit residual represents a gain; the clearing entry must debit Disposal.

modules.title: Inventory valuation: FIFO & AVCO
modules.summary: Track cost layers, calculate averages and understand why LIFO is only a comparison.

sections.title: FIFO follows the oldest costs
sections.text: First in, first out assigns the oldest available purchase costs to units sold. Closing inventory therefore contains the most recent costs. It is a cost-flow assumption, not necessarily a description of which physical items moved. With rising prices, FIFO generally gives lower cost of sales and higher closing inventory than LIFO, all else equal.
sections.new: Picture trays arriving in a queue. FIFO takes costs from the front of the queue first; the newest tray costs remain on the shelf.

sections.title: State which average you use
sections.text: Periodic weighted-average cost = total cost of goods available ÷ total units available for the period. Moving AVCO recalculates average after each receipt and uses that average for the next issue. They can differ if sales occur between purchases. These questions specify periodic or moving average where it matters; retain unrounded values until the final answer.
sections.new: Average the costs using the number of units, not just the price labels. Ten cheap units and one expensive unit are not two equally sized batches.

sections.title: Cost is not the only limit
sections.text: Inventory is generally measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV). NRV is expected selling price less costs to complete and sell. LIFO assigns newest costs to sales but is not permitted under IAS 2 or FRS 102; it is covered here only to interpret the lecture notes.
sections.new: If damaged stock will bring in less than its cost after selling costs, keeping the old higher figure would overstate the asset.

example.prompt: Buy 10 units at £4 then 10 at £6. Sell 12 units after both purchases. Assume NRV exceeds cost.
steps: Periodic AVCO: total cost £100 ÷ 20 = £5 per unit.
AVCO cost of sales: 12 × £5 = £60; closing inventory: 8 × £5 = £40.
example.result: Under each method, cost of sales + closing inventory = £100 total cost.

modules.watch: LIFO appears in the source notes, but do not present it as an acceptable IFRS/FRS 102 accounting policy.

terms.definition: First-in-first-out cost assignment: oldest purchase costs go to issues first.
Estimated selling price less estimated costs of completion and sale.

reading.topics: Inventory valuation; FIFO; weighted average; lower of cost and NRV

questions.q: Under FIFO, which costs go to sales first?
questions.explain: First in, first out issues the earliest available costs first.
questions.hint: Read the words behind the acronym.

questions.q: Buy 10 units at £2, then 10 at £3. Sell 12 after both purchases. FIFO cost of sales?
questions.explain: 10 × £2 + 2 × £3 = £26. Eight £3 units remain.
questions.hint: Use all ten oldest units, then two from the newer batch.

questions.q: 10 units at £2 and 30 at £4. Periodic weighted-average unit cost?
questions.explain: Total cost £20 + £120 = £140 over 40 units gives £3.50 per unit.
questions.hint: Weight each price by its number of units.

questions.q: Is LIFO an allowed inventory cost formula under IAS 2 or FRS 102?
questions.explain: LIFO is not permitted under IAS 2 or FRS 102. It is included here for comparison with the notes.
questions.hint: Knowing a method exists does not mean standards allow it.

questions.q: Inventory cost is £700; NRV is £620. At what value is it reported?
questions.explain: Use the lower of cost and NRV, so write down inventory by £80 to £620.
questions.hint: The measurement rule places a ceiling at recoverable net selling value.

questions.q: With rising purchase prices, FIFO closing inventory contains mainly:
questions.explain: FIFO sells the oldest cost layers, leaving newer cost layers in inventory.
questions.hint: What remains after the oldest layer has been issued?

questions.q: Buy 20 units at £5 and 10 at £8; then sell 24. Periodic AVCO closing inventory?
questions.explain: Total cost £180 ÷ 30 = £6 per unit. Six units remain: 6 × £6 = £36.
questions.hint: Calculate weighted-average cost, then apply it to unsold units.

questions.q: Moving AVCO: 10 units at £4; sell 5; buy 5 at £6. New average after the receipt?
questions.explain: Five old units cost £20; five new cost £30. £50 ÷ 10 units = £5.00.
questions.hint: Only the units still held enter the new moving average.

modules.title: Warranties & deferred grants
modules.summary: Estimate obligations and release deferred income without counting things twice.

sections.title: A warranty can create a present obligation
sections.text: A provision is a liability of uncertain timing or amount. In the simple warranty examples, past sales create a present obligation, an outflow is probable and a reliable estimate can be made. Expected warranty cost = units sold × expected claim rate × average cost per claim. Warranty expense is recognised with the provision.
sections.new: The business sold goods with a promise to fix defects. It does not know which customers will claim, but it can estimate the overall cost of keeping that promise.

sections.title: Separate recognising from using a provision
sections.text: Recognise Dr Warranty expense, Cr Warranty provision. When actual covered repair costs are paid, Dr Warranty provision, Cr Bank. This uses the liability instead of charging the same expense again. Review the required closing estimate at year-end and adjust any shortfall or excess.
sections.new: First record the expected obligation. Later, paying a valid claim reduces that obligation. The payment is not automatically a second warranty expense.

sections.title: Release a deferred grant as specified
sections.text: These exercises assume a grant for future related costs is initially deferred: Dr Bank, Cr Deferred grant income. Release the matching portion: Dr Deferred grant income, Cr Grant income. If costs and conditions are even across four years, release one quarter each year. Different grant standards or conditions can require different treatment.
sections.new: The liability is like a waiting room for income that is not recognised yet. As the stated conditions and related costs are met, the relevant part leaves the waiting room and becomes income.

example.prompt: Sell 1,000 appliances with a 3% expected claim rate. Average claim cost £40. Separately, receive an £8,000 grant covering four equal years of qualifying costs.
steps: Dr Warranty expense £1,200; Cr Warranty provision £1,200.
A £100 covered claim: Dr Warranty provision £100; Cr Bank £100.
Grant receipt: Dr Bank £8,000; Cr Deferred grant income £8,000. First year's release: Dr Deferred grant income £2,000; Cr Grant income £2,000.
example.result: After that release, deferred grant income is £6,000, assuming all conditions are met.

modules.watch: Use the average cost of a claim, not the selling price of the product. A provision is a liability, not a pot of saved cash.

terms.definition: A liability of uncertain timing or amount, recognised when the required criteria are met.
Grant receipts not yet recognised as income under the assumed deferral model.

reading.topics: Recognition concepts; income deferrals; company reporting. Consult the book index for provisions, warranties and government grants; no dedicated chapter is asserted.

questions.q: 500 products, 4% expected claims, £30 average cost per claim. Expected warranty cost?
questions.hint: Find the expected number of claims first.

questions.q: Recognise a £900 warranty obligation. Which journal?
options: Dr Warranty expense; Cr Warranty provision
questions.explain: The obligation creates a liability and an expense now, before claims are paid.
questions.hint: Recognise the estimated cost and the obligation together.

questions.q: Pay £80 for a covered claim against an existing warranty provision. Which entry?
options: Dr Warranty expense; Cr Bank again
questions.explain: Use the provision: debit it to reduce the liability and credit bank.
questions.hint: The expense was already estimated when the provision was recognised.

questions.q: What distinguishes a provision from a precisely invoiced payable?
options: It can never be a liability
Its timing or amount is uncertain
questions.explain: A provision is an estimated liability whose timing or amount is uncertain.
questions.hint: Think uncertainty in the obligation, not absence of an obligation.

questions.q: A £12,000 grant is deferred and released over three equal qualifying years. Annual income?
questions.explain: £12,000 ÷ 3 = £4,000 recognised per year under the stated assumptions.
questions.hint: Allocate the grant across the specified equal periods.

questions.q: Which journal releases £2,000 of deferred grant income?
options: Dr Bank; Cr Deferred grant income
Dr Deferred grant income; Cr Grant income
questions.explain: Debit the liability to reduce the deferred balance and credit income for the portion earned.
questions.hint: No new cash arrives on release.

questions.q: Warranty provision opens at £1,000. Claims paid £300. Required closing provision £900. Additional expense?
questions.explain: After claims, £700 remains. Top up by £200 to reach the required £900.
questions.hint: Subtract claims from the existing provision before comparing with the new estimate.

questions.q: A £15,000 grant covers five equal years. After two full qualifying years, the deferred balance is:
questions.explain: Annual income is £3,000. After £6,000 has been released, £9,000 remains deferred.
questions.hint: Distinguish cumulative income from the unreleased balance.

modules.title: Loan repayments: principal versus interest
modules.summary: Split a repayment correctly and understand the limits of a simplified method.

sections.title: Receiving a loan and repaying it are different
sections.text: At set-up, Dr Bank, Cr Loan payable for the amount borrowed. At repayment, bank is credited. A payment containing both principal and interest needs two debits: Dr Loan payable for principal, Dr Interest expense for interest, Cr Bank for the total. The notes' last set-up label actually describes this repayment entry.
sections.new: When you borrow, money comes in and a debt appears. When you repay, some money clears the debt and some pays the borrowing cost.

sections.title: A simplified equal-allocation exercise
sections.text: Only where explicitly assumed: total payments = monthly payment × number of payments; total interest = total payments − original principal. Divide total interest equally across payments, then principal per payment = payment − interest per payment. This is a classroom simplification, not a general amortised-cost rule.
sections.new: The question gives you permission to split interest evenly. Do not carry that shortcut into a question that gives an interest rate on the outstanding balance.

sections.title: When interest is based on the outstanding balance
sections.text: Under an effective-interest approach, interest for the period = opening loan carrying amount × effective periodic interest rate. Principal repaid = cash payment − interest. Closing loan = opening loan + interest − payment. With level payments, interest normally falls and principal repaid rises as the loan balance falls.
sections.new: If the debt gets smaller, applying the same rate to it gives less interest. That leaves more of the next payment available to clear principal.

example.prompt: Borrow £1,200 and repay £110 monthly for 12 months. The question explicitly assumes equal allocation of total interest.
steps: Monthly entry: Dr Loan payable £100; Dr Interest expense £10; Cr Bank £110.
example.result: After 3 payments, loan principal is £900 under this simplified assumption.

modules.watch: Do not apply both flat interest and effective interest in the same exercise. Follow the method and periodic rate specified in the question.

terms.definition: Interest allocated using a rate applied to the opening amortised-cost balance.
The part of a loan payment that reduces principal, not the interest cost.

reading.topics: Loan liabilities; finance expenses; company finance. Use lecture notes for the equal-allocation convention; no dedicated amortised-cost chapter is asserted.

questions.q: A payment is £150 principal and £20 interest. What is credited to Bank?
questions.explain: The bank pays the combined amount: £150 + £20 = £170.
questions.hint: Cash includes both components.

questions.q: Which debit reduces the loan liability during repayment?
questions.explain: Debit Loan payable for principal repaid. Debit Interest expense separately for interest.
questions.hint: A liability is reduced by a debit to that liability.

questions.q: Borrow £2,000; total repayments £2,300. Ignoring fees, total interest is:
questions.explain: £2,300 paid back − £2,000 principal = £300 interest over the loan.
questions.hint: Subtract what was originally borrowed from all repayments.

questions.q: Equal-allocation assumption: total interest £240 over 24 monthly payments. Interest per month?
questions.explain: £240 ÷ 24 = £10 monthly interest under this explicitly simplified method.
questions.hint: Allocate the total charge across the number of payments.

questions.q: A £125 payment includes £15 interest. Principal repaid?
questions.explain: £125 − £15 = £110 reduces the liability.
questions.hint: The rest of the cash after interest clears principal.

questions.q: At the initial receipt of a new loan, which entry is correct?
questions.explain: Borrowing increases bank and the liability. It is not a repayment or revenue.
questions.hint: Cash comes in and an obligation to repay appears.

questions.q: Opening loan £1,000; monthly effective interest 1%; payment £110. Closing loan?
questions.explain: Interest is £10. £100 of the payment repays principal, so closing loan is £900.
questions.hint: Opening balance + interest − cash payment.

questions.q: Under level payments and effective interest on a falling loan balance, which pattern is normal?
options: Interest falls and principal repaid rises
questions.explain: A constant rate on a smaller balance produces less interest, leaving more of each level payment for principal.
questions.hint: Apply the same rate to a smaller opening debt.

modules.title: Pulling it together: statement notes
modules.summary: Reconcile retained earnings, inventory and non-current asset movements.

sections.title: Retained earnings roll forward
sections.text: Closing retained earnings = opening retained earnings + profit for the year − dividends, with losses reducing the balance. The supplied notes use opening plus profit; that assumes no distributions or other adjustments. Capital contributions are not retained profit. These company equity records are separate from sole trader drawings examples.
sections.new: Retained earnings are profits kept in the company over time. A year's profit adds to the total; a distribution takes some away.

sections.title: Explain what inventory contains
sections.text: A manufacturer's inventory note can list raw materials, work in progress and finished goods, then total them. The amounts should reflect the stated valuation basis, including any needed NRV write-down. Do not include trade receivables or equipment as inventory.
sections.new: A note opens the inventory total into useful boxes: not started, partly made and ready to sell.

sections.title: Reconcile cost and accumulated depreciation separately
sections.text: Closing asset cost = opening cost + additions − original cost of disposals. Closing accumulated depreciation = opening accumulated depreciation + current charge − accumulated depreciation on disposals. Closing NBV = closing cost − closing accumulated depreciation. Prior-year NBV uses opening figures. Sale proceeds are not the amount removed from cost.
sections.new: Use two movement bridges: one for original cost and one for depreciation charged so far. Subtract the final totals only after completing both bridges.

example.prompt: Equipment: opening cost £20,000; additions £5,000; disposed cost £4,000. Opening accumulated depreciation £8,000; current charge £3,000; depreciation on disposal £2,500.
example.result: Remove the sold asset's cost and its own accumulated depreciation, not its sale proceeds.

modules.watch: Statement notes should reconcile to the financial statements. An apparently reasonable total is not enough if the movements do not reconcile.

terms.definition: Cumulative profits retained in the company after distributions and other relevant movements.
A bridge explaining how an opening amount becomes the closing amount.

reading.topics: Statement presentation; non-current asset notes; companies and retained earnings

questions.q: Opening retained earnings £4,000 and profit £1,500, with no distributions. Closing retained earnings?
questions.explain: Opening retained earnings plus profit: £4,000 + £1,500 = £5,500.
questions.hint: Profit retained adds to the opening balance.

questions.q: Raw materials £200, work in progress £350, finished goods £450. Total inventory?
questions.hint: Include all three stages of production.

questions.q: Opening asset cost £10,000, additions £3,000, disposed original cost £2,000. Closing cost?
questions.hint: Add new cost, remove disposed original cost.

questions.q: Opening accumulated depreciation £4,000, charge £1,500, depreciation on disposals £800. Closing balance?
questions.hint: Remove the accumulated depreciation belonging to sold assets.

questions.q: Closing cost £18,000 and closing accumulated depreciation £7,000. Closing NBV?
questions.explain: NBV = cost − accumulated depreciation = £11,000.
questions.hint: Do not add the contra-asset balance to cost.

questions.q: In the cost movement note, what amount is removed on disposal?
questions.explain: The cost column removes original cost. Accumulated depreciation is removed in its own section.
questions.hint: Cost and proceeds are different pieces of the disposal calculation.

questions.q: Opening retained earnings £6,000; loss £800; dividends £500. Closing retained earnings?
questions.hint: A loss and a distribution both reduce retained earnings.

questions.q: Opening cost £30,000, additions £4,000, disposed cost £6,000. Opening depreciation £12,000, charge £3,000, disposed depreciation £4,500. Closing NBV?
questions.explain: Closing cost £28,000; closing accumulated depreciation £10,500. NBV = £17,500.
questions.hint: Complete the cost and depreciation bridges separately.
